#9800. AutoSynthData: Generating Training Data for Enterprise Agents

Enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments. The work they ask these agents to do is shaped by the systems they use, the rules they follow, and the state of their data. A model may be broadly capable and still struggle with a particular environment: a workflow it handles poorly, a combination of tools it misuses, or a constraint it fails to respect. Those are the weaknesses an enterprise needs to improve.

The difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data. An individual failure tells us something, but training a model requires many new tasks that exercise the same capability in different situations. Those tasks must also be possible to complete in the environment, resemble work someone would actually request, and have a reliable way to check whether the agent succeeded.

At ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data. It uses a target model’s failures and a stronger teacher’s successes to decide what the model should learn next, then generates and validates new tasks that exercise those capabilities. As the model improves, the curriculum shifts toward what it still finds difficult. We illustrate the pipeline with EnterpriseOps Gym (Malay et al., 2026), using the released dataset. We begin by describing the environment an agent operates in and what makes a task useful for training.

An agentic environment defines the world in which an agent operates: the state it can observe and modify, the tools and APIs it can invoke, and the state transitions produced by its actions.

A task is instantiated within this environment. We use the following abstraction:

The system specification defines the constraints under which the agent operates, including system instructions, environment policies, and, when applicable, task-specific initialization such as a seeded database state or a set of knowledge articles.

The specification must be compatible with the environment’s tools, state, and supported actions. Its instructions should be clear and avoid arbitrary constraints introduced solely to manufacture difficulty.

The user prompt specifies what the user wants the agent to accomplish, together with any user-level constraints. A generated task should satisfy three properties.

Feasibility. There should exist at least one trajectory in the current environment that satisfies the user prompt while respecting the system specification. This rules out tasks that depend on unavailable tools, inaccessible knowledge, impossible state transitions, or actions prohibited by policy.

Realism. The user prompt should resemble something a user would plausibly ask in the target environment. The space of executable behaviors is usually much larger than the space of realistic workflows.

Difficulty. For training, the task should expose a weakness of the current agent. Tasks that are already solved reliably provide little new training signal. The useful region is therefore tasks that are feasible and realistic, but not yet consistently solved.

The verifier determines whether the resulting trajectory successfully completes the task. It should satisfy three properties.

Consistency. It should agree with the user prompt, the system specification, and the task-specific environment state.

Soundness. It should reject trajectories that fail to satisfy the task or violate relevant constraints.

Completeness. It should accept valid solutions rather than encode one particular reference trajectory.

These properties matter directly during training. A lax verifier can reward incorrect behavior, while an overly restrictive verifier can penalize valid solutions.

Given an environment and a target model, AutoSynthData generates training tasks consisting of a system specification, user prompt, and verifier. The generated tasks are grounded in the environment and selected to provide useful training signal for the current model.

AutoSynthData first evaluates the target model in the environment using diagnostic tasks and identifies patterns in the tasks it struggles to complete. A stronger teacher helps characterize which of those tasks are solvable and what successful behavior looks like. AutoSynthData turns the resulting capability gaps into new executable tasks, checks each task in the environment, and uses accepted samples for post-training. Evaluating the updated model reveals which gaps remain and can guide the next round of generation.

AutoSynthData uses evaluation runs in the target environment to identify what the model needs to learn next. In our EnterpriseOps Gym experiment, we run both the target model and a stronger teacher on the evaluation tasks. We examine those runs to identify:

We distill these findings into sanitized capability specification cards. The evaluation tasks guide what the model should learn, but the generator does not receive their original prompts, entities, trajectories, or verifier details. It receives the cards and uses them to create new tasks with different prompts, states, and solution paths.

Identifying a capability gap tells us what to teach, but training requires many varied tasks that exercise it. AutoSynthData uses the specification card to generate those tasks.

Suppose the target model struggles with tasks that require the following workflow:

The generator creates new tasks that exercise this workflow, varying the entities, initial environment state, workflow composition, tool combinations, wording, and difficulty. The stronger teacher then demonstrates a successful trajectory for each task. For supervised fine-tuning (SFT), these demonstrations teach the target model how to apply the capability in new situations.

AutoSynthData builds the dataset in two phases: first generating and validating core samples, then expanding them into novel variants.

The target phase creates the core set of training samples from the capability specifications. Workers generate independent tasks in parallel, picking up a new target when they finish. Each candidate goes through validation, execution, solver evaluation, and repair before acceptance. The result is a batch of vetted examples built around what the target model needs to learn.

The multiply phase expands the dataset by creating novel variants of accepted target samples. Each variant has its own user request, environment state, entity configuration, reference trajectory, and verifier, and must pass the same validation and execution checks. A multiplied sample cannot seed another multiplied sample. This anchors expansion to the vetted target set and limits drift across generations.

To support both phases, AutoSynthData separates generation control from environment-specific execution. A shared controller coordinates generation, quality control, coverage, and dataset construction, while an adapter handles environment execution, task and state management, reference replay, deterministic verification, solver execution, and task profiling.

Together, parallel target generation and multiplication provide a path to training-scale datasets. Their usefulness depends on the checks applied to every candidate: the task must be executable, the solution must work, and the verifier must distinguish success from failure.

Generating a plausible request is not enough to produce useful training data. A task may be impossible in the target environment, its reference solution may fail when executed, or its verifier may reward the wrong final state. AutoSynthData checks these properties before accepting a task for training.

AutoSynthData reviews quality at two levels: individual candidates must pass verification, and batches must provide useful coverage and diversity.

Each candidate must clear a quality-control loop before entering the training dataset. We begin with solver evaluation to measure difficulty. In the configuration used here, we favor tasks the target model solves on no more than one of three trials and the stronger solver solves on at least two of three trials. Candidates also undergo positive and negative verification and a bounded repair process.

The positive gate asks: Does the intended solution solve the generated task?

The pipeline executes the reference trajectory in the target environment and checks the resulting state against the candidate’s verifier. This reveals mismatches among the prompt, initial state, solution, and success criteria.

The negative gate asks: Do relevant incorrect outcomes fail?

For example, it can mutate parts of the expected outcome and confirm that those states no longer pass verification. This catches weak verifiers that award success without requiring the intended behavior.

Failed candidates go to a critic before being discarded. The critic examines the sample and its failure, looking for inconsistent state, impossible workflows, incorrect task construction, bad reference trajectories, weak verifier logic, or a mismatch with the intended capability. The critic’s findings guide repairs, with a fixed limit on retries:

A repaired task must pass the relevant checks again. The diagnosis guides repairs to the existing candidate rather than requiring generation to start over.

Passing these checks makes a sample eligible for training, but individually valid samples can still form a repetitive or unbalanced dataset. AutoSynthData therefore also reviews generation at the batch level.

A batch may overrepresent a few easy task families, miss a capability, or reflect too much generation effort spent on a low-yield pattern.

A meta-review examines accepted samples, rejected samples, and generation behavior across each batch. It asks:

The controller tracks coverage in the accepted dataset, reduces generation in overrepresented regions, and directs more work toward gaps. When a region repeatedly produces poor candidates, critiques and meta-review guide changes to the generation strategy. These adjustments balance useful learning signal, task quality, coverage, diversity, and low redundancy within the available generation budget and dataset size requirements.

Together, these feedback loops improve both individual tasks and the dataset they form: sample-level checks guide candidate repair, while batch-level review guides future generation.

The useful training distribution changes as the model improves. AutoSynthData treats synthetic data generation as a search for tasks near the target model's capability boundary: difficult enough to expose weaknesses, but solvable enough for the teacher to provide reliable demonstrations.

After post-training, we evaluate the updated model in the same environment. Tasks it now solves reliably are less useful for the next training round; persistent failures point to capabilities that still need attention. Those results can guide the next generation round.

Our experiments focus on SFT, but the same mechanism could support reinforcement learning (RL): generate tasks that challenge the current policy and provide reliable learning signal, train, then move the generation target with the updated policy. We plan to test this moving, difficulty-calibrated frontier beyond SFT.

We use EnterpriseOps Gym to test whether this approach improves a model on tasks in a stateful enterprise environment. We generate training tasks in the Gym’s Hybrid and ITSM environments, fine-tune the target model on accepted samples, and evaluate the resulting checkpoints.

We tested the pipeline on the Hybrid domain of EnterpriseOps Gym using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and Qwen3.8-27B as the teacher.

AutoSynthData generated 2,000 synthetic training samples in about 18 hours. We fine-tuned Gemma on this dataset and evaluated the resulting checkpoints on the benchmark. The best checkpoint was epoch 5.

The synthetic SFT checkpoint improves mean Pass@1 by 7.2 percentage points, a 35% relative improvement, and raises verifier success from 63.01% to 68.55%. It closes 59% of the original Pass@1 gap between Gemma and the reference model.

The training tasks were newly generated from capability specifications; the generator did not receive the original evaluation tasks. The result demonstrates improvement in EnterpriseOps Gym Hybrid, the environment used for this experiment.

We also applied AutoSynthData to the ITSM domain of EnterpriseOps Gym, using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash as the teacher. AutoSynthData generated 1,994 synthetic training samples in 66 hours. Generation took longer than in the subsequent Hybrid run described above, primarily because the ITSM run used a larger teacher model and preceded pipeline optimizations that improved throughput.

On ITSM, synthetic SFT raises mean Pass@1 from 18.77% to 27.18%, showing that the approach also improves performance in a second domain.

The tasks most useful for training depend on both the environment and the model working in it. AutoSynthData uses the model’s failures to choose what to generate, validates new tasks against the environment, and makes those tasks available for post-training. Our EnterpriseOps Gym results show the value of that approach in a controlled setting. As the model changes, the same process can focus on the gaps that remain.

InfoQ Homepage News Vercel Launched Experimental Board to Coordinate Tasks Across Humans and Coding Agents

Nov 25, 2026 2 min read

Vercel has launched Vercel Board, an experimental, headless message board where people and coding agents coordinate tasks across tools and harnesses. Vercel says Claude Code, Codex, Pi, OpenCode, eve, fx, Mastra, and LangChain can work on the same board as if they were a single harness.

Each Vercel team gets a default board, named General, organized into channels and threads. Developers and agents read and write through the `vercel board` CLI or the `@vercel/board` JavaScript SDK. A skill, installed with npx skills add vercel/board --skill board, teaches coding agents the CLI. Agents name themselves with --as or BOARD_PROFILE, but still act with the operator's or project's credentials.

A task is a thread whose state the board keeps. A worker claims a ready task, posts updates, and completes or fails it. A claim is a lease of up to five minutes and must be renewed; if it expires, the task returns to the queue. When two workers claim the same task, one succeeds and the other fails with task_claimed. Tasks can declare dependencies, so a review waits until its fix completes while independent work proceeds in parallel. Watchers on a Vercel deployment can run when a reply is posted or a label changes, waking the deployment so no process has to stay running.

Sync, configured in the SDK and delivered through Vercel Connect, can attach a board channel to Slack, GitHub, or Linear. Slack and Linear sync both ways; GitHub imports pull requests and issues and does not write back unless the project sends those messages. Grants control who can read, post, and manage each channel. For an agent in a Vercel Sandbox, sandboxPolicy() can grant limited board access without putting a credential inside the sandbox. Vercel says it rebuilt v0's software factory on Board, and that the factory now merges over 50% of its pull requests.

Official documentation warns that Board grants do not apply on Slack, GitHub, or Linear, so a private Slack channel synced into an open board channel is readable by the whole Vercel team.

Austin King (@MadeWithOzten) replied to Vercel's announcement asking to

Do this self-hosted and open source - Rust, Yjs Sync,

then wrote that he had bought openboard.lol

For a self-hosted open source Vercel board like thing.

Aaron Delz (@AaronDelz) said he already kept a shared checklist with his agent, and liked that a Board task can be completed with the pull request attached:

Same rule my agents run on: no saying 'done' without the evidence.

Similar coordination shows up elsewhere. OpenCrawl is an open source, self-hostable board that also records agent sessions. GitHub Agent HQ can assign issues and pull requests to Copilot, Claude, or Codex. Linear's cloud coding agent turns scoped issues into draft pull requests with Claude Code or Codex. Claude Code agent teams coordinate multiple Claude Code sessions around a shared task list, and the Agent2Agent protocol standardizes delegation between agents rather than hosting a board.

Board remains experimental infrastructure on a Vercel team. Setup steps and the CLI and SDK references are in Vercel's Board documentation

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

#9798. Entering the Geminispace

November 25, 2026 · About 13 minutes · Tags: blogsystem5, gemini

This article was originally published on Substack in the Blog System/5 newsletter and is replicated here for archival purposes.

On May 1st, 2020, Project Gemini made the rounds for the first time via a Hacker News discussion thread. I remember seeing the announcement back then, barely a month after the Covid 19 worldwide lockdown, and thinking it was a cool gimmick. But that was that.

However, I’ve recently been seeing a few gemini:// links here and there as footers in hand-crafted blogs, and I nerd-snipped myself to export this blog as a Gemini capsule that you can find at gemini://capsule.jmmv.dev/. The process has been fun, and I actually quite like the extreme minimalism of the resulting site. So what else would you expect from me? I had to write about it—hence this post.

Today we’ll learn a little bit about what Gemini is, how I approached the blog export to its native gemtext format, and I’ll confess a couple of… sins I committed along the way.

A blog on operating systems, programming languages, testing, build systems, my own software projects and even personal productivity. Specifics include FreeBSD, Linux, Rust, Bazel and EndBASIC.

A terrible name, that is. Looking for information about Gemini these days is extremely hard, thanks to Google polluting the namespace with its own AI offering. Of course that’s not Project Gemini’s fault because Google’s thing came after them, but still, good luck finding stuff about this network.

Joking aside, let’s look at Project Gemini’s barebones front page:

… and break down the introductory and only paragraph:

Gemini is a new internet technology supporting an electronic library of interconnected text documents.

You can think of Gemini as a way to access a bunch of text-only pages, with links among them, so you can find information and follow links to additional resources. Instead of using http:// or https:// URL prefixes, you use gemini:// instead.

That’s not a new idea, but it’s not old fashioned either.

Exactly. Gemini is like the WWW, or “the web” in more colloquial/modern parlance. In fact, Gemini is a parallel community to the web. Obviously, that’s not a new idea because the web dates back to 1989, and we are now 37 years after that.

The idea is not unique either because Gopher, a much lesser-known option, exists as well. Surprisingly to me, I realized that Gopher came after the web in 1991 while researching this article. I had always assumed Gopher was first and that the web came to replace it because of Gopher’s rigidness. But that’s not quite what happened.

It’s timeless, and deserves tools which treat it as a first class concept, not a vestigial corner case.

Humans have shared written documents since around 3400–3100 BCE (roughly 5,100–5,400 years ago) in ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt, and that’s probably (hopefully?) not going away. It’s true, though, that at this point, text sharing is not the primary thing that the web does, as you well know. We have morphed the web from a document distribution tool into an app platform, for better or worse.

A little confession: I worked at Google for 12 years, starting right at the time they published Google Wave (2009), which to me marked the start of truly interactive web apps—more so than Gmail (2004) did. In the back of my mind, I knew I was helping turn the web into how we run apps, destroying the traditional desktop paradigm—a feeling I never liked. And… it happened. Obviously, it’d have happened without me, a little pawn in the game, but it bothered me regardless.

Gemini isn’t about innovation or disruption, it’s about providing some respite for those who feel the internet has been disrupted enough already.

(That comma splice hurts.) As we have established earlier, Gemini’s ideas are not new, so it’s indeed not innovative. And seeing how little people read these days, or even how unable to pay attention to long-form text they are, it’s not going to disrupt anything either. But respite is key: having a separate place where you know you’ll only find some sort of counter-culture sounds entertaining.

Fun fact: I wasn’t quite sure what respite meant and originally took it to be similar to spite. That meaning would have worked equally well here, if not better?

Here is the interesting thing. Gemini claims that it has been designed to minimize the chances of becoming bloated, and I’m not exactly sure how you can prevent that. For example: articles can provide links to images, but images are not auto-loaded. OK, says who? The auto-loading part is something the client browser controls, and it’d be trivial to create a Gemini browser, or modify an existing one, to auto-load and render images. That’d go against the spirit of Gemini, but if enough people wanted it, it’d happen. Same story as the browser wars.

And that’s the key: “enough people”. As long as Gemini stays under the radar and only like-minded people gravitate towards it, these properties will be maintained. But if for any reason it becomes more mainstream… unwanted changes will happen.

Gemtext is the native format of documents stored in the Gemini network, with a MIME type of text/gemini and a .gmi extension. Gemtext documents are typically grouped in capsules—which is just another name for “website”.

The format itself is like a super-diluted version of Markdown, supporting just these features:

Workable for sure, but weak. In my opinion, Gemini missed the boat of creating a truly semantical web, but for that you need additional primitives to represent more concepts. In any case, you can read through the long FAQ to know that this was discussed and eventually ruled against, so know that a lot of thought was put into its design.

Yet another fun fact: just two days ago, I stumbled upon “Good morning and welcome to my idea of a new web”: the proposal of a “browser” that just renders Markdown documents. This feels quite similar to the idea behind Gemini, but using a better (not a great) format with more markup abilities. And I say fun fact because, as I was learning about Gemini, I was imagining developing this exact alternate idea.

One curious bit is that Gemtext is also the format for subscription feeds. Sure, you can offer an RSS feed for your capsule, but RSS is a monster spec that feels out of place in a minimalistic network like Gemini’s. So you can abuse Gemtext to create a feed by creating a page that’s primarily links with a de-facto YYYY-MM-DD Title format. Again, it’s simple, and it works.

The big benefit of Gemtext’s simplicity is that clients can also be super-simple. You can rest assured that all clients will be able to display the same content, consistently. So far I’ve tried Elpher within Emacs, Lagrange on the desktop, and Buran on my Android phone. All are simple. All display text in the same way.

I definitely do not recommend using the Gemtext format to persist your original content, but that doesn’t mean you have to write in Gemtext. Which brings us to Markdown again.

All of the content you are reading in this blog is authored and stored as Markdown documents. Like many other people who still maintain a blog in this day and age, I started with a hosted platform (Blogger) and then experimented with Medium. But as soon as Medium became riddled with noise, I ran away. Unfortunately, escaping was difficult: the format that Medium spit out was frigging awful—almost as if it were designed to provide the illusion that you could export content, even if the content was nearly useless after the fact.

It was at that point that I committed to converting my golden copies to Markdown even though authoring in Markdown was more inconvenient. And believe me: it is inconvenient, especially when having to insert images. But now I own my content in a format that’ll survive for years to come.

Which brings us back to Gemtext. The thought that crossed my mind when I stumbled upon Project Gemini again three weeks ago and that triggered this whole thing was: can I write a script to convert my Markdown docs into a capsule? And with “I” I really mean AI, because this is the kind of experiment I was not going to code myself.

And of course I could. After just one simple prompt, I had a converted site that I could browse. Granted: the conversion Python script was literally awful, and the converted format was not great either, but having something I could play with inspired me to try harder.

So I threw everything away and started over, again with AI, to write a conversion tool for my blog (codenamed gengems for now) that takes the existing Hugo layout and spits out a capsule end-to-end in just 300 milliseconds while processing 1000 documents. The tool is obviously written in Rust, and by now supports enough configurable features that I’m increasingly tempted to throw Hugo away for the web version and create my own static site generator too. Because, you know, while Hugo works, it isn’t the greatest in usability and its recurrent incompatible changes are annoying. I’ll resist the urge to do that for now… I think.

Let’s dive a tiny bit into gengems. First of all, this second iteration is still entirely vibecoded. Oops, first sin. I have not looked at the code because it’s working for what I need it to do, it’s fast, and it’s not going to be used by anyone else… unless you want it, but then I’d probably rewrite it once more now that I know what the final feature set looks like.

Now, for this second iteration, I was so close to running out of my $20 weekly OpenAI quota that I pivoted from my favorite GPT 6.1 Sol model to GPT 6 Luna to see how far I could go. Luna is so cheap that you can do a ton with it, and I actually got gengems to work well enough within just a few iterations.

But oh dear. Luna is cheap, but it’s also kind of crap for coding. It stops half-way. It doesn’t think through enough corner cases. It doesn’t produce enough tests. The plans it produces are very vague. You have to be extremely prescriptive when asking it to do things and even that leads to mixed results. Out of curiosity, when my weekly cap was reset, I asked Sol to review what Luna did, and oh boy did it have things to say. From design problems to important missing tests, passing through outright bugs. I let it fix those issues, and I continued building with Sol.

Right now, I’m actually pretty happy with the results of gengems. I can configure the mapping of pages to templates in a much more explicit way than in Hugo. I can use MiniJinja for templating. I can specify cross-site links. I can handle inline links, figures, and even tables. I can generate archives/feeds for the site, for each year, for each month. I can process blog posts, and also standalone pages. All in all, the results are very satisfactory given the close-to-zero effort I put into it.

With the site exported to Gemtext, I needed a server. There are a lot of options out there, but the one that piqued my interest was Agate: a minimalistic Gemini server written, of course, in Rust. You run the binary pointing it at the directory containing the generated site and, voila, it works. Agate even takes care of auto-generating SSL certificates because all Gemini traffic is TLS-protected, and the fact that it’s automated is a relief because dealing with certificates is a pain.

But running Agate once, interactively, and making it serve in the background are different stories. I am running FreeBSD on my server and I could have used the prebuilt agate package, but then I encountered a crashing bug and wanted to add a feature, so I had to pivot to building from source. And, as you can imagine, Cargo leaves a lot to be desired if you want to install the resulting product to a running system.

Now, of course you can copy the built binary to, say, /usr/local/bin/agate, but there is typically much more than a binary in a distribution: think about documents, examples and, for a server program in particular, startup scripts. Mind you, Agate’s source tree does include a FreeBSD rc.d script, but it was buggy, insufficient, and it also required manual copying. So I created a PR to revamp the installation system based on earlier experience with setting up similar infrastructure in other Rust services I run.

I mentioned briefly above that I wanted to add a feature to Agate and that it was the reason I had to build from source. And that feature is… analytics, which are the second sin right there.

But wait a second. What are analytics? You do realize that Agate prints and saves a log of incoming connections (with IPs redacted by default), right? That’s par for the course for any Internet server out there, because in order to serve requests… well, the server actually needs to know what those requests are and where to send the responses to. So you can always analyze the log to gain some insights on traffic.

And that’s pretty much what I did. I just wired this exact same information to my own analytics service for visualization. The only thing I see are the pages that are being downloaded, when they are downloaded, and the originating country (computed from the requester’s IP after truncating the last octet to mask it). Essentially… good old page counters from the 1990s.

The way I implemented this is generic though: I extended Agate to add optional support for an SSI-style URL inclusion primitive and then added such a call to the capsule-wide footer template given to my Gemtext generator. As a high-level primitive, it can serve other purposes, like sourcing comments for each page by making the footer download a pre-rendered .gmi chunk. I haven’t implemented that yet in my comments service, but it should be pretty easy.

Sounds interesting? I might try to contribute this SSI feature upstream to Agate, but I predict that this collides with the goal of a lightweight server and that it’ll be rejected. But I’ll try anyway. I want to get the FreeBSD-related bug fixes and related improvements merged first, because those are helpful to everyone, I hope.

That’s about it! If you are in the U.S. you are about to have 4 days off, so spend that time falling into the Gemini rathole. And if you are elsewhere, do the same! It’s entertaining.

From now on, remember that you can also read this blog via gemini://capsule.jmmv.dev/ if you want a super-fast, distraction-free experience. To get started, visit the Gemini software page for a long list of clients to choose from and install.

(Content also available at: gemini://capsule.jmmv.dev/post/2026/11/entering-the-geminispace.gmi)

#9796. 'TheMailer' Phishing Kit Puts AI in the Driver's Seat

The commercial kit uses attacker-supplied AI models to personalize lures, evade spam filters, and scale campaigns to tens of thousands of targets.

A new phishing kit is capable of orchestrating most elements of the attack through AI functionality, including tailoring email lures specifically to bypass content filters.

That's according to new Varonis research detailing "TheMailer," a phishing kit that leverages large language models (LLM) to a degree hardly seen in the cybercriminal ecosystem. Phishing kits and phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) platforms have gained significant popularity in recent years, and AI has only made them more capable. To date, phishing kit AI functionality focuses mostly on generating lures, coding realistic phishing websites, conducting reconnaissance, and automating simple repetitive tasks.

TheMailer distinguishes itself in two primary ways. One, it automates much of the phishing process from end to end using the attacker's chosen AI model. Two, as Varonis senior security researcher Daniel Kelley wrote in the blog post, the kit can tailor lures to each mail provider and "rewrite them until they bypass spam filters."

Related:Webworm APT Slithers Into Networks With Customized SoftEther VPN

The attacker's "customer journey" begins by buying a lifetime license for between $3,000 and $6,000 in cryptocurrency (depending on the deal and which AI functions are included). The customer operator then plugs in their API key, selects an AI model (Claude, ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Grok, Gemini, and Mistral are included), and then they're more or less ready to start conducting campaigns. Kelley noted that customers only need to bring SMTP servers, proxies, and target email lists.

TheMailer can generate lures from a short prompt or a real brand email, personalize the emails for each recipient (including email address, body, and subject line), remove AI writing patterns, and adjust content for spam filters.

Kelley tells Dark Reading the kit is built to scale against targets.

"The seller's screenshots show a single campaign of nearly 25,000 emails and a list of more than 145,000 targets being sorted by mail provider. What's different is that every recipient gets their own version of the email, subject line, and attachment, so a bulk campaign no longer looks like one," he says. "I wouldn't call it a spear-phishing tool. The personalization we saw is at the level of a name on an invoice, and we didn't see features for researching individual targets. It's opportunistic phishing with the polish of something targeted."

It's unclear how successful the kit is — attacker LLM tools are historically capable of undertaking tasks at scale, but the success rates of these tasks vary — though Varonis assesses TheMailer to have a large customer base. Moreover, the kit may be a sign of things to come.

Related:Anthropic Finds Ingredients for Future AI Worms

"I'd expect more kits to follow," Kelley says, "because once one seller offers this, buyers start asking for it elsewhere."

For defenders, Varonis offered a few main recommendations. Because TheMailer is built specifically to get past content filters, organizations should consider email authentication practices like SPF, DKIM, and DMARC enforcement; monitoring for lookalike and new domains; and checking links through full redirect chains at the time of the click.

And when conducting phishing training, Varonis recommends making it reflect how emails look in a post-AI world.

"Bad grammar isn't a reliable sign anymore, so teach users to be wary of urgency, unexpected requests, and login prompts, especially 'unusual activity' or account statement alerts," the blog post read. Finally, "Least-privilege access and data monitoring limit the damage if someone clicks anyway."

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. After cutting his teeth writing for independent gaming publications as a teenager, he graduated from Emerson College in 2016 with a Bachelor of Science in journalism. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

He has received numerous awards, including TechTarget's Writer of the Year in 2022 as well as more than 10 Azbee awards for his reporting between 2022 and today.

#9795. The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed.

Microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row. It is now available through Hugging Face.

Figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind. From our ThinkingBox paper.

A customer writes in. Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date.

The AI agent does careful work. Nine tool calls: it pulls the order, checks tracking, looks up her customer profile, searches the refund policy twice, confirms no ticket exists, opens one, documents the timeline, and reads the policy correctly; her account segment genuinely does not qualify for late-delivery compensation.

Then it closes the ticket as resolved and replies “ Since your query is resolved, is there anything I may assist you with? ”

Two things are wrong. The carrier exception is still open, so the required end state was on hold, pending resolution. And the customer never got a real answer to what she actually asked.

An AI grader checking tool calls would see nine well-formed ones. The grader checking whether the agent wrote to the database would see that too. The database is what disagrees.

That gap is what ThinkingBox measures. Across 507 stateful business workflows, each run 20 times against various LLM models, it grades agents on terminal backend state and side effects. This post covers what we found, what consistency costs, and how to run the benchmark yourself through OpenEnv.

You can run this one yourself: the example above is adapted from a benchmark task sandbox_external_retail_group1.py:test_case_ST003_006, and the executable check that fails is a single field: the ticket's status is solved where the required end state is hold. The full trace is in Appendix D.4, Case 3 of our paper.

Want to try it before reading the results? Skip to section Run it yourself.

Final responses and valid tool calls are only proxies. An agent can sound correct while leaving the wrong value, changing the wrong record, or creating an extra side effect. Only the records it leaves behind settle the question.

The gap is substantial. In a common-set ablation covering 121,680 valid trials across 12 LLM models, 79,853 attempts failed the executable checks. Of those failures, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error. Executable checks nevertheless found wrong field values in 77.61% of them, unintended extra effects in 43.30%, and missing required effects in 25.36%. Those state-check findings overlap.

A trajectory is a claim. Database state is the evidence. Repetition is the trust test.

An agent that processes a refund correctly once and mishandles it the next four times is not a working refund agent. So every task runs 20 independent times, each from an identical clean backend, and we report three different things:

Table 1: The three numbers we report, and the question each one answers.

We use observed 20/20 in this blog post as the literal count of how many of the 507 tasks passed 20 out of 20. No estimator, no smoothing.

Starting with the familiar view. The table below reports pass@1, the single-attempt score estimate, broken out by domain. This is the number most leaderboards publish, and on its own it reads like an ordinary capability ranking.

Table 2: ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain. Each model is evaluated on every task for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the group leader; underline marks the runner-up. The standard errors for the single attempt score estimates are provided in Table 4 in our ThinkingBox paper.

Claude Opus 5.5 leads overall at 67.16%, two-thirds of a point above Claude Opus 5. Kimi-K3 is the strongest open-weights model, within a point of GPT-6-Astra. Domain matters just as much: Claude Opus 4.6 scores 68.62% on retail but 8.30% on auto insurance.

One good run tells you a model can do the work. It does not tell you whether it will do it again. So run every task 20 times and ask how much of that score survives.

Figure 2: How much of each model's single-attempt score survives 20 repeats.

Only three hold on to most of their pass@1 scores: GPT-6 Astra retains 78% of its single-attempt rate, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Opus 5 each retain 71%. At the other end, GLM-5.1, Kimi-K2.6 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro each keep about 8%.

The gap between what a model can do once and what it does every time is the whole story.

Figure 3: Breadth and consistency pull apart. Twelve of the eighteen models are shown; six below 33% pass@1 are omitted for legibility.

Kimi-K3 has the broadest coverage of any model we tested. It solves 93.89% of the benchmark at least once: 476 of 507 tasks. Only 31 tasks defeat it entirely, the lowest count in the field. On retail workflows it leads outright at 82.24% pass@1, ahead of every proprietary model.

Kimi-K3 is also among the least consistent. Just 68 of 507 tasks, 13.41%, succeed in all 20 attempts.

Claude Opus 5 inverts this. It solves fewer tasks at least once (79.09%; 106 defeat it entirely) but completes 47.53% of the benchmark on every single attempt.

A newer model does not fix this. Claude Opus 5.5 scores higher than Claude Opus 5 on every-attempt average, 67.16% against 66.50%, and solves more tasks at least once. It passes exactly the same number of tasks on all 20 attempts: 241. Half a point of headline accuracy bought no additional dependability at all.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches real records, pass@20 is the wrong column to look at.

Capability comparisons usually stop at the score. For anyone deploying, the relevant question is what a successful unit of work costs. We measure that as cost per successful task attempt. We say task attempt because every benchmark task is run repeatedly and cost is incurred per attempt, so pass@1 is the matching quality denominator.

We took each model's recorded token usage from its full 507 × 20 campaign and priced it at undiscounted list rates available on OpenRouter+, reversing promotional discounts and excluding endpoints that declare quantization. Input, output and cache rates all come from one provider endpoint per model.

Then we divided one run's cost by the number of attempts that succeeded:

Cost per successful task attempt = estimated cost for 507 attempts, one per task ÷ (507 × pass@1)

This is a comparative efficiency index, not an invoice, and not the price of serving one production request. It also prices single successes, not consistency. We price consistency next.

Example: GPT-5.4 costs $43.49 for 507 attempts (one attempt per task) and has 65.36% pass@1, so $43.49 ÷ (507 × 0.6536) = $0.131 per successful task attempt.

A model is on the frontier if no other model is both no more expensive and at least as accurate. Three models qualify; every other model is dominated on at least one axis.

Figure 4: Cost per successful task attempt against pass@1. Ringed dots are pareto cost frontier models.

The frontier has three steps. GPT-5.6 Sol has the lowest cost per success at $0.127; GPT-5.4 raises pass@1 by 3.45 percentage points for $0.004 more per success; Claude Opus 5.5 adds another 1.80 points at $0.276 per success. Each of the three remains on the cost frontier line because no cheaper model matches its pass@1.

Claude Opus 5 is the clearest case: at $0.475 per successful attempt and 66.50% pass@1, it is both more expensive and less accurate than Claude Opus 5.5 at $0.276 and 67.16%.

Cost per success rewards a model that is cheap and often right. It does not reward a model that is right every time. So we also compute cost per dependable task: the cost of the full 20-run campaign divided by the number of tasks the model passed on all 20 attempts.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of 20 runs of 507 attempts ÷ tasks passing 20/20

Example: GPT-6-Astra costs 20 × $86.03 = $1,720.60 for the campaign and passes 231 tasks on every attempt, so $1,720.60 ÷ 231 = $7.45 per dependable task.

Table 3: The nine lowest costs per dependable task among models with at least one observed 20/20 task, sorted low to high. Estimated $, not actual cloud bills.

Now rank by consistency. GPT-5.4 is the cheapest at $6.80, though only 128 tasks meet the bar. GPT-6 Astra reaches 231 at $7.45, and Claude Opus 5.5 the joint-highest 241 at $7.80.

None of the three dominates the others: each additional dependable task costs more. Claude Opus 5 also passes 241, but at $13.30, so Opus 5.5 dominates it outright. GPT-5.6 Sol, the cheapest per single success at $0.127, costs $9.76 per dependable task. The cheapest way to get a right answer is not the cheapest way to get a dependable one.

We assign each failed trace one deterministic diagnostic signature, and the headline is actionable: roughly four in five failures are tool handling, not reasoning. Across an ablation study in Table 5 of our paper:

These are unweighted averages of per-model shares and observable labels, not unique causal explanations.

The practical pattern is simple: agents usually get far enough to attempt the workflow, then fail to recover from tool errors, failed preconditions, or empty lookups. That is a retry and error-recovery problem before it is a model problem.

Difficulty also changes by domain: across the models listed in Table 2 above, retail averages 59.52% pass@1 while auto insurance averages 33.83%.

What to do about it. Treat the 20/20 rate as a design input, not a verdict. The same signal the benchmark grades on is available in production: check the terminal state before you commit, not the model's summary of it.

Classify tool and system errors so retries target the recoverable ones. Cut the tool surface to what the workflow needs. And require human approval on the changes you cannot cheaply reverse. We have not measured the lift from any of these on this benchmark, which is exactly the kind of thing the environment now makes testable.

ThinkingBox is the agent sandbox, while ThinkingBox-Bench is a dataset benchmark to evaluate agents. The diagram at the top of this post shows the loop; here is what each part does.

Figure 5: The sandbox loop from panel A in Figure 1 above: isolated tool session, terminal database state, side effects, executable judges.

Each task defines a starting backend state, a user goal, the available MCP tools, the domain policy, and executable checks over the terminal state. A simulated user holds private context (a booking reference, a preference, or a date of birth) and releases it only when asked.

Every attempt gets an isolated MCP session with freshly initialized state. Two attempts of the same task never share a database row or cached tool state, which is what makes 20-trial comparison meaningful.

At the end, a side-effect extractor derives what actually changed, and deterministic judges compare it against the required end state, accepting any trajectory that produces the right outcome while rejecting wrong, missing or extra effects. For requirements with no clean database value ("did the agent disclose this is not guaranteed?"), a narrow binary rubric question handles the semantics. 477 of the 507 tasks are graded on state alone; 30 add response rubrics.

The trust boundary: the model sees tasks, dialogue and tool schemas. Golden state, assertions, grading internals and credentials stay on the evaluator side.

ThinkingBox is now on Hugging Face, both the harness and the dataset. ThinkingBox-Bench now sits behind the OpenEnv interface, and each finished episode returns a binary pass/fail reward. The released adapter is designed for evaluation; separate, non-benchmark scenarios can use the same interface in training workflows.

Tested on Linux and WSL, with Python 3.11+, uv and Docker. You also need a thinkingbox-data checkout at the pinned release and model endpoints for the agent, simulated user and judge. One endpoint can serve all three roles, which is the simplest way to start. The OpenEnv image starts only the OpenEnv API; everything else you run yourself.

In a second terminal, start Typesense 30.1 and wait for its health check:

In a third terminal, start the Session Proxy and MCP servers.

Back in the first terminal, start the OpenEnv server against a ThinkingBox YAML config naming your three models (config guide):

Gate on readiness before running anything. It returns 503 until its observable data, configuration and Session Proxy checks pass. It cannot observe Typesense or live-probe every model endpoint, so confirm those separately:

Now score a real episode. example_usage.py only resets and lists tools; for agent actions, effects and assertions use the packaged evaluator:

The OpenEnv adapter writes operational failures to an errors sidecar so they can be rerun rather than silently mixed with model outcomes. A canonical result must resolve or explicitly account for those attempts; we counted system errors as unsuccessful trials.

Runs are gated on a pinned framework commit, a pinned data release and a bundle hash, so a canonical result is verifiable rather than asserted.

The useful part of this work is not our pass@1 leaderboard. It is the environment.

If you are evaluating an agent that touches real records:

Further details can be found in the following links:

ThinkingBox code is MIT-licensed; the benchmark data is CDLA-Permissive-2.0; the OpenEnv environment ships under OpenEnv's BSD-3-Clause.

Disclaimer: every task in the public benchmark is a synthetic reconstruction. The workflows and policies are modeled on real AI agentic enterprise patterns; the customers are not real.

ThinkingBox and ThinkingBox-Bench is built by the Microsoft Copilot Studio team in partnership with Toloka with collaborators from the University of Pittsburgh, Northwestern University, Columbia University and UC Irvine who interned at Microsoft. Questions are welcome in the comments section below or on github or by email at firstnamelastname@microsoft.com.

+ OpenRouter cost snapshot taken on Sept 20th 2026; Opus 5.5 pricing as per the Anthropic site.

ST003_006 delegates its pass check to validate_database. Unequal result and golden database hashes fail even when diff is empty. The diff explains a failure; it does not decide the pass.

This small replay exercises the released function with four authored effect inputs. Run python3 reproduce.py. It verifies the source pin and tests supplied hashes; it does not calculate a database hash, run an agent, or reproduce the full environment.

AI-assisted source reading and example by CyberNative AI LLC.

The useful cut is agent-reported "done" versus backend terminal state.

A green success from the same process that acted is a claim, not a grade. I'd want the eval to score durable side effects (ticket status, refund state, policy-cited fields) against a frozen oracle — and fail when the narrative is green while the database disagrees.

Practical check: can a run be marked done when the terminal-state fixture is red?

#9793. Beyls: Wrapping up LLVM's relicensing effort

Kristof Beyls has published a summary to the LLVM discussion forum to announce that the project is declaring success and bringing its relicensing effort to a close after eight years.

We've been asking past contributors to relicense their work since 2018. New contributions have come in under Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception since January 19, 2019. Code contributed before that date was under LLVM's earlier licenses (UIUC/NCSA, plus MIT for some runtime libraries), so we needed permission from its authors to move it over. [...]

Today, more than 99.5% of all lines of code ever contributed to LLVM are either covered by the new license, too small for copyright to apply, or no longer in the repository.

Rather than trying to "chase the last tiny fraction forever" LLVM is winding up the effort. Any contributors with code contributed before January 19, 2019 who have not signed a relicensing agreement and do not want their contributions made available under Apache-2.0 with the LLVM-exception can still reach out to the project to ensure their code has the appropriate SPDX license identifier.

Posted Nov 21, 2026 13:13 UTC (Sat) by coriordan (guest, #7544) [Link] (1 responses)

The LLVM exception: https://merlijn.sebrechts.be/blog/what-is-the-apache-2-ll... It says two things. (Based on my quick read; corrections welcome) 1. That Apache-2 licensed compilers (which insert some compiler code into the executables they create) don't create Apache-2 obligations for the programs they create. 2. It fixes incompatibility with GPLv2 by saying that, for a combined work of Apache-2 plus GPLv2 code, if an authority decides that any clause of Apache-2 is incompatible with GPLv2 then that clause of Apache-2 doesn't apply. (Which I guess they decided is fine because the places where there could be conflicts, such as patents, using the GPLv2 version isn't enough of a problem to be worth incompatibility.) So, the LLVM exception looks like a pretty good instrument.

#9792. Optimizely Malware Attacks Highlight Third-Party Vendor Risks

At least 178 organizations, including several major brands, unwittingly exposed website visitors to hydra-like malware via a third-party platform.

Some of the world's most recognizable brands unwittingly became conduits for malware this week, after an attacker slipped malicious code into website testing scripts delivered by Optimizely, a platform that allows organizations to experiment with and optimize their online presence.

The attack potentially exposed visitors to sites operated by at least 178 organizations — including Zoom, CNN, Salesforce, and IKEA — to malware capable of stealing payment card details, hijacking cryptocurrency transactions, and delivering exploit kits for iPhones and iPads.

Many organizations use Optimizely to run website experiments, test different page designs and personalize content for visitors. To do this, Optimizely embeds scripts in customer websites that can serve different versions of a page or its content to visitors, track their interactions, and measure which versions perform best.

Related:It's a Bot World. We're Just Living in It

The attackers appear to have exploited this mechanism to insert malicious code into a custom field called Project JavaScript, which allows Optimizely customers to run their own code across website pages.

British Web security monitoring service Report URI, among the first to detect the activity, documented the tampering but said it could not determine how the attackers gained the ability to modify customer projects. "We don't know how the attacker got write access to so many unrelated customer projects: a compromised Optimizely system, a compromised credential with cross-customer access, or something else. That's for Optimizely to explain," Report URL founder Scott Helme wrote.

Report URI said it located and examined 1,611 unique Optimizely scripts. It found malicious code in 188 scripts associated with 178 organizations. The company has published a list of the affected websites on its site, grouped by industry sector.

Optimizely itself has said little about the incident so far besides acknowledging it and pinning it somewhat vaguely to a vulnerability in the platform's Experimentation account sign-up flow. "We've fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code from affected projects. We've also taken steps to secure affected user accounts and put additional protections in place to prevent unauthorized code from being delivered," the company said.

Related:Satellites Have a Ground-Level Cybersecurity Problem

In a follow-up statement to Dark Reading, Optimizely spokesperson identified these measures as including "blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts." The company has also implemented "additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation," the statement read. Optimizely however, did not respond to a Dark Reading question on how a vulnerability in the account sign-up flow could have given an attacker write access to customer projects.

"That’s the question every affected customer should be putting to Optimizely right now," says Justin Beals, CEO and founder of Strike Graph. "They need to know how a new account got write access to other tenants' projects, which project IDs were changed and when, and whether that path is fully closed."

Until Optimizely explains the authorization failure, customers can't judge whether the company's reported fix addresses the cause or just the symptom, he says.

Related:What We Missed: Nvidia CEO Scandal Rocks AI Industry

The incident is a reminder that organizations need strict controls over third-party scripts running on their websites, Beals adds. Most organizations approve a third-party vendor script once during procurement and never revisit it later. Optimizely, for instance, passed whatever review the 178 affected companies ran, and the malicious code still shipped from Optimizely's own CDN under its own certificate.

"The takeaway is that a vendor approval is a point-in-time decision, and the risk changes every time that vendor’s code changes," Beals says. "You can keep using these tools if you decide where they’re allowed to run."

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security R&D at Fortra, says incidents like these show why organizations implement a browser security feature called Subresource Integrity (SRI) to verify that externally hosted files, such as JavaScript, haven't been altered before they are loaded and executed.

"The problem that we have here is that you may include a file in your website that is safe for months or even years and then, unbeknownst to you, a breach occurs within your vendor and that 'file that's been safe forever' is suddenly no longer safe," Reguly says.

SRI allows organizations to perform version pinning based on file hashes to protect against attacks like the one that went down at Optimizely. "The downside is that it requires a bit more effort and management to maintain your Web pages, which are often seen as 'set it and forget it' resources," Reguly adds.

Chris Nyhuis, CEO of Vigilant, says Optimizely demonstrates what happens when trust becomes an attack surface. "Organizations allowed a third party to deliver executable code into their customers' browsers, and that trust was exploited," he says.

The answer isn't to eliminate third-party technology but to eliminate "blind trust," Nyhuis says. "Restrict where vendor scripts execute, limit their access to sensitive data, monitor their behavior and changes, and independently validate what they're doing."

Furthermore, Optimizely also needs to explain how a flaw in an account sign-up process allowed an attacker to modify executable code belonging to 178 unrelated customers. "For that to happen, there had to be a path around customer authorization boundaries," he says. "Whether that involved broken tenant isolation, privilege escalation, an authorization flaw, or access to an overly privileged service remains to be established by the forensic investigation."

This article was updated at 1 p.m. ET on Nov. 18 to reflect a statement from Optimizely.

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9790. Introducing Falcon ASR

Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%

We’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect. Developed at the Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in Abu Dhabi, it also supports English, French, Spanish and Portuguese.

In our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used. On our internal Emirati evaluation, it recorded the lowest word and character error rates among the systems we compared.

We also support word-level timestamps for transcriptions, linking each transcribed word to its position in the audio.

Arabic speech varies by region, speaker and setting. A model that handles a formal news broadcast may still struggle with a conversation in Emirati or with speech recorded over a phone line. Dialectal Arabic also has fewer transcribed resources than Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), which makes training and evaluation harder.

We trained Falcon-ASR on Emirati, MSA, other Gulf and Arabic dialects, and English. Our aim is to transcribe the words people use in everyday speech, including dialectal forms and changes between languages.

The Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard, maintained by the ELM Research Center, ranks systems by the equal-weight average WER across six test sets. It also reports character error rate (CER). Lower values are better for both metrics. Our Falcon-ASR evaluation follows this protocol.

WER = Word Error Rate; CER = Character Error Rate. A lower value indicates better performance.

We evaluated Falcon-ASR on the same six benchmarks using the leaderboard’s pinned manifests. Competitor figures are the published leaderboard averages checked on 30 September 2026. Falcon-ASR’s average WER is 2.25 percentage points better than the best published result in that snapshot.

Public evaluation data already includes Emirati: Casablanca has a UAE subset. We complement that coverage with an internal evaluation of additional Emirati and Gulf speech, using held-out recordings and human-validated transcripts to assess transcription accuracy beyond the public UAE subset.

In our internal Emirati evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved 22.73% WER and 10.19% CER:

Falcon-ASR has the lowest WER and CER among the systems compared here. Its WER is 4.07 percentage points below Qwen3-Omni, the next best result. The results show improved transcription accuracy at both the word and character level on this evaluation.

We included background noise, overlapping speech, music, room reverberation and telephony effects, as well as variations in speed and pitch. We applied the same treatment to Emirati recordings, exposing the model to a range of conditions it may encounter in meetings, calls and other everyday recordings.

Falcon-ASR also transcribes English with the same model weights. In our evaluation on the seven public English test sets used by the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard, it achieved a mean WER of 5.74%.

The model also supports French, Spanish and Portuguese. All five languages use the same weights, without requiring a language flag. The output is a transcript in the language spoken.

Falcon-ASR builds on our Falcon3-Audio work. The architecture and training approach for Falcon3-Audio are described in Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data.

Our Hugging Face Demo Space lets you try Falcon-ASR and explore its transcription capabilities. API access and native applications are planned. We invite you to try the Demo with your own recordings.

We thank the team behind the Falcon-Emirati model for their support with Arabic foundation models. Read about their latest work in the Falcon-Emirati blog post.

We also extend our sincere thanks to Mikhail Lubinets for continued support with the compute infrastructure.

نقدّم Falcon-ASR، نموذجنا للتعرف على الكلام العربي بحجم 1.6 مليار معلمة، مع اهتمام خاص باللهجة الإماراتية. طوّرنا النموذج في معهد الابتكار التكنولوجي (TII) في أبوظبي، وهو يدعم أيضًا اللغات الإنجليزية والفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية.

في تقييمنا، حقق Falcon-ASR متوسط معدل خطأ في الكلمات بلغ 20.92% عبر ست مجموعات اختبار باللغة العربية، مقارنةً بأفضل نتيجة منشورة بلغت 23.17% في نسخة لوحة المتصدرين التي استخدمناها. وفي تقييمنا الداخلي للهجة الإماراتية، سجّل النموذج أدنى معدلات خطأ في الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة التي قارناها.

ندعم أيضاً الطوابع الزمنية على مستوى الكلمات في عمليات التفريغ النصي، بحيث ترتبط كل كلمة بموضعها في التسجيل الصوتي.

يختلف الكلام العربي باختلاف المنطقة والمتحدث وظروف التسجيل. فقد ينجح نموذج في تفريغ نشرة إخبارية رسمية، ثم يجد صعوبة في تفريغ محادثة باللهجة الإماراتية أو تسجيل عبر الهاتف. كما أن الموارد الصوتية المفرّغة نصيًا للهجات العربية أقل من تلك المتاحة للعربية الفصحى، مما يزيد صعوبة التدريب والتقييم.

درّبنا Falcon-ASR على اللهجة الإماراتية والعربية الفصحى ولهجات خليجية وعربية أخرى، إلى جانب الإنجليزية. وهدفنا هو تفريغ الكلمات التي يستخدمها الناس في حديثهم اليومي، بما في ذلك الصيغ اللهجية والانتقال بين اللغات.

ترتّب لوحة المتصدرين المفتوحة الشاملة للتعرف على الكلام العربي، التي يديرها مركز ELM للأبحاث، الأنظمة وفق متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات عبر ست مجموعات اختبار، بوزن متساوٍ لكل مجموعة. وتعرض أيضًا معدل خطأ الأحرف (CER). وكلما انخفضت قيمة أي من المقياسين، كان الأداء أفضل. ويتبع تقييمنا للنموذج هذا البروتوكول.

WER هو معدل خطأ الكلمات؛ وCER هو معدل خطأ الأحرف. تشير القيمة الأقل إلى أداء أفضل.

قيّمنا Falcon-ASR على مجموعات الاختبار الست نفسها، باستخدام قوائم العينات المثبّتة في لوحة المتصدرين. وأرقام النماذج المنافسة هي المتوسطات المنشورة في اللوحة، والتي جرى التحقق منها في 30 سبتمبر 2026. وكان متوسط خطأ الكلمات للنموذج أفضل بمقدار 2.25 نقطة مئوية من أفضل نتيجة منشورة في تلك النسخة.

تتوافر بالفعل بيانات عامة لتقييم اللهجة الإماراتية، إذ تضم مجموعة Casablanca قسمًا خاصًا بالإمارات. ونكمّل هذه التغطية بتقييم داخلي لتسجيلات إضافية من الكلام الإماراتي والخليجي، باستخدام تسجيلات مخصّصة للاختبار ونصوص مرجعية خضعت لمراجعة بشرية، لتقييم دقة التفريغ على مواد إضافية إلى جانب البيانات الإماراتية العامة.

حقق Falcon-ASR في تقييمنا الإماراتي الداخلي معدل خطأ كلمات قدره 22.73٪ ومعدل خطأ أحرف قدره 10.19٪:

سجّل Falcon-ASR أقل معدل لخطأ الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة المقارَنة هنا. وكان معدل خطأ الكلمات أقل بمقدار 4.07 نقطة مئوية من Qwen3-Omni، صاحب النتيجة التالية. وتُظهر النتائج تحسنًا في دقة التفريغ على مستوى الكلمات والأحرف في هذا التقييم.

ضمّنا بيانات التدريب ضوضاء خلفية وكلامًا متداخلًا وموسيقى وصدى الصوت وتأثيرات الاتصالات الهاتفية، إلى جانب تغيّرات في سرعة الكلام وحدّة الصوت. وطبّقنا المعالجة نفسها على التسجيلات الإماراتية، لتهيئة النموذج للتعامل مع ظروف مختلفة قد يواجهها في الاجتماعات والمكالمات والتسجيلات اليومية الأخرى.

يفرّغ Falcon-ASR الكلام الإنجليزي باستخدام أوزان النموذج نفسها. وفي تقييمنا على مجموعات الاختبار الإنجليزية العامة السبع المستخدمة في لوحة Hugging Face المفتوحة للتعرف على الكلام، بلغ متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات 5.74٪.

يدعم النموذج أيضًا الفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية. وتستخدم اللغات الخمس أوزانًا واحدة، دون الحاجة إلى تحديد اللغة مسبقًا. ويكون الناتج تفريغًا نصيًا باللغة المنطوقة.

يستند Falcon-ASR إلى أعمالنا في Falcon3-Audio. وتعرض ورقة Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data بنية Falcon3-Audio ونهج تدريبه.

يتيح عرضنا التجريبي على Hugging Face تجربة Falcon-ASR واستكشاف قدراته في تفريغ الكلام. أما الوصول عبر واجهة API والتطبيقات الأصلية فهو مخطّط له. ندعوكم إلى تجربة النموذج باستخدام تسجيلاتكم.

نتوجّه بجزيل الشكر إلى الفريق القائم على تطوير نموذج Falcon-Emirati على دعمهم في مجال النماذج التأسيسية للغة العربية. ويمكن الاطّلاع على أحدث أعمال الفريق من خلال المقال المنشور حول Falcon-Emirati.

كما نتقدّم بخالص الشكر والتقدير إلى Mikhail Lubinets على دعمه المستمر للبنية التحتية الحاسوبية.

#9787. Major Brazilian Signature Apps Enable RCE & Fraud

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Government-sanctioned authentication middleware is used for exceptionally important legal documents, yet it's often rife with RCE bugs.

Brazil's digital certificate system was recently found to be rife with vulnerabilities in browser extensions used by millions of government agencies and legal, medical, and tax professionals.

That's the assessment of researchers at Bay Area Labs, who this week flagged five particularly popular digital extensions that allow Brazilian citizens and institutions to not only sign official documents, but sign them with the greatest possible degree of trust issued by their government. All five of them possessed vulnerabilities which could've allowed attacker-controlled websites to run arbitrary code on users' machines.

One can only hope that the researchers, who disclosed the vulnerabilities this week, were the first to discover them. Remote code execution (RCE) in this context could have allowed fraudsters to sign legal documents in victims' names, and hackers to breach major government organizations (as well as professionals who manage large amounts of personal, financial, tax, and health information on behalf of their clients).

Related:'God Mode' Flaws Could Wreak Border-Control Havoc

On Sept. 23, 2020, Brazil's National Congress enacted Federal Law No. 14,063. 14,063 laid the ground rules on how individuals and organizations could digitally sign documents when dealing with public institutions. Among other things, it delineated three tiers of trust that an electronic signature could carry: "simple," "advanced," and "qualified." "Qualified" meant that a digital signature would be equivalent to a notarized, handwritten one. It would be sufficient for high-stakes legal proceedings, like real estate transfers and electronic tax processes. And any digital signature backed with an ICP-Brasil certificate — ICP-Brasil is the country's official national public key infrastructure (PKI) framework — would be considered "qualified."

Brazilian government institutions, tax professionals, and anyone in-between who wants to provide a qualified digital signature for a sensitive legal document online can use browser extensions like Lacuna Web PKI, Softplan Web Signer, Certisign WebSigner, Certisign CertiPlugin, and BRy Assinatura Digital. Each of these tools lets official government and vendor portals read ICP-Brasil certificates, to confirm that signers are who they say they are, and put pen to Web page.

These tools will also engage with non-official websites. So if an attacker can lure a victim to their own site — or, in some cases, plant a malicious ad or iframe on a legitimate site — they can engage that victim's authentication middleware. Only one of the five extensions, CertiPlugin, had any kind of allowlist, yet it included any domain ending in ".one," meaning that an attacker would simply need to purchase a domain with that common and freely available suffix in order to perform an attack.

Related:Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era

The core issue endemic to each of these five extensions, and others used by other national governments, is that they allow websites to dictate the dynamic link libraries (DLLs) they load. Loading cryptographic libraries is a normal part of the way these apps work. But if they don't properly check that a loaded file is trusted? In that case, an attacker that lures a victim to their site can trigger a malware download and then instruct the victim's signing software to load that malware as if it were a legitimate library.

All five extensions' RCE vulnerabilities earned "critical" 9.6 scores in the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS). Each of them was patched as of mid-September, but lessons remain.

Lacuna Web PKI, Softplan Web Signer, Certisign WebSigner, Certisign CertiPlugin, and BRy Assinatura Digital have more than 10 million installs between them.

Among that user base are some of the most significant, high-value organizations and professionals in the country. On its website, Lacuna alone counts Brazil's Federal Senate, its National Council of Justice, its navy, and its stock exchange among its clients "who trust our work." These extensions are far from limited to major government agencies, of course. BRy advertises its work with the University of São Paulo, the São Paulo metro, and one of the country's few biggest banks, Caixa Econômica Federal.

Related:Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem

Attackers could have used the vulnerable authentication middleware to infect employees at major state institutions and, in Arnott's words, "cause mayhem." As an easier alternative, they could target middle class professionals: lawyers, doctors, accountants and so on. An accountant might manage digital signing credentials for hundreds of different individuals and businesses on their single computer. An attacker with that accountant's access could then impersonate those people and companies in legally significant transactions — forging agreements, submitting false tax filings ... the sky's the limit.

"It's really interesting how these signing tools always consistently have the same critical vulnerabilities," Arnott marvels, after having found characteristically similar vulnerabilities in extensions used by Belgium, Sweden, and Qatar's governments in recent months. "Since they are security tools, you'd expect them to be properly built. But they're so often making the same mistake, by allowing any site to pick which DLLs to load. I imagine it's to reduce friction so organizations can more easily load in the drivers for hardware security tokens and readers, because the driver DLLs aren't always known to the signing tool vendor or signed properly with Authenticode. It is insane to me how many independent vendors make this same mistake though."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.
